item.title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98005ndz7no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control - Published "This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack." The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away. Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed. It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz. Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war. We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close. Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting. It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire. "Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line. He told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals. "I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway." He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too. At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach. "We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said. Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled. The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region. Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions. Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha. We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based. About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side. As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle. We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city. Taiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen. Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons. Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically. There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line. "It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said. The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces. Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. In the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied. Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby. She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up. A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said. About 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents. We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days. Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day. "We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me. Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain. "We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added. Fatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing." Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said. She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said. "I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God." A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since. On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war. It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months. item.title: Seoul summons Ukraine envoy over North Korean prisoner-of-war row
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8ly40xx0dr0o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Seoul summons Ukraine envoy over North Korean prisoner-of-war row - Published South Korea has summoned Ukraine's acting ambassador after President Volodymyr Zelensky last week announced his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo lodged a formal complaint with Andrii Vieshkin and expressed "strong regret" that Zelensky had revealed the transfer, which Seoul says was supposed to be a secret. The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. President Lee Jae Myung called the disclosure "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. Ukraine's foreign ministry declined to comment when approached by the BBC. In early 2025, Ukraine said its forces had captured two North Korean soldiers as prisoners of war in Russia's Kursk Oblast. After more than a year of negotiations between Seoul and Kyiv, Zelensky announced they had been transferred to South Korea at the UN General Assembly last Wednesday - adding they had not been "easy to capture alive". Seoul confirmed the news but sharply criticised Zelensky for allegedly breaking an agreement to keep the transfer a secret. This was partly to protect the North Koreans' families, President Lee's office said in a statement, which added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. Seoul demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. Lee faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure. The South Korean opposition accused him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. Lee, whose party takes a conciliatory approach to the North, has been making efforts to reopen peace talks, with little success. Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. "When North Korea actively participates in a war in Europe, South Korea cannot remain a distant observer," said Mykhailo Podolyak, a senior adviser to Zelensky. "The transfer of defence technologies and capabilities from Seoul to Kyiv is not just about helping Ukraine; it is about South Korea protecting its own long-term security interests by containing the expansion of an aggressive totalitarian axis." This July, Seoul announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang. Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko - Published11 January 2025

item.title: Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m27dprvzv7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far - Published Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months. The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police. Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer. The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa. Here's what we know. Busisiwe Mahlangu Case 1 Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties. Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed. Itumeleng Kekana Case 2 Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026. The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park. No arrests have been made so far. Nomfesane Mjobo Case 3 Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park. Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises. No arrests have been made. Unknown woman Case 4 Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear. No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made. Gracious Nkomo Case 5 Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area. Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death. Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo Case 6 Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park. Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case. Unidentified woman Case 7 Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed. No arrests have been made. Dineo Motapane Case 8 The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive. Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni. She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case. Jabulile Ntimba Case 9 The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni. According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence. The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice. Ntombifuthi Nxumalo Case 10 The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body. This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death. A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge. Unidentified woman Case 11 The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni. The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area. The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared. No arrests have been made. Boitumelo Gift Mashita Case 12 Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken. Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand. Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies. While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September. The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg. It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni. President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience". South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day. Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests. item.title: French PM warns against escalation of school protests after 164 arrested
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmqxvnn49rg2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
French PM warns against escalation of school protests after 164 arrested - Published France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", following the arrests of 164 people on Monday. The demonstrations, which started in Paris and have seen teenagers blockading their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers." But a French union that defends the interests of high school students said the protests were a "legitimate response" to the conditions they face. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 12 members of the security forces, 12 students and three school staff were injured on Monday, while 180 schools were affected. He did not provide further details on those who had been arrested. The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris. Incidents of vandalism were reported, along with fireworks being aimed at police, and the protests have now spread to other regions in France. According to the AFP news agency, four high schools were reportedly blockaded in the southern regions of Alpes-Maritimes and Var. Protests have also been reported in Marseille, the northern Lille area and Sedan in the north-eastern Ardennes. The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, defended the protests in a post on social media. "Lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classes, stress caused by Parcoursup [the web platform used in France for students to apply to the first year of higher education]... These issues are by no means inevitable, but simply the result of 10 years of Macron's policies and the lack of resources in the national education system," it said. It called on students to blockade schools on Tuesday in defence of "their rights and against budget austerity". On the same day, unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants also called for a day of walkouts to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions. In response to the student movement, Lecornu said "the difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed", but that "violence must be condemned unequivocally, and its perpetrators must answer for their actions". The prime minister also accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of urging students to expand the movement. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, LFI's leader, blamed the Lecornu government for having "ordered the crackdown" on the protest, adding that the high school students taking part were "harmless". But Nuñez said the demonstrations and blockades were "not very typical protest movements". "It is much more like urban violence, with a number of individuals who were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes, equipped with projectiles, who clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces," he said. "It wasn't about making demands; it was really violence in its purest form." Since the protests began, several incidents involving violence between students and police officers have been reported. In one incident, a police officer reportedly fired a round from a grenade launcher used for crowd control, injuring a high school student, according to France's BFMTV. Investigations have been launched into these incidents, the broadcaster added. - Published3 days ago - Published18 September - Published16 September

item.title: Nigerian attempts to break world record by dancing non-stop for seven days
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8r6z2gjzd1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nigerian attempts to break world record by dancing non-stop for seven days - Published A Nigerian dancer is attempting to dance non-stop for seven days in order to set a new world record. Benjamin Daniel, known as Ben Dancer, is aiming to dance for 168 hours - 41 hours longer than the current record for the longest individual dance marathon. Guinness World Records has yet to confirm whether the attempt qualifies as an official record. The BBC has contacted the organisation for comment. Young people have been gathering in recent days to cheer him on at Freedom Park in Lagos, filming his every move and dancing along from behind the barriers. "It's a beautiful moment. Seeing how far he has come and witnessing him achieve this feat made me incredibly proud and grateful to God," Uche Anumudu, one of those watching, told the BBC. The current record is 127 hours, set by Indian dancer Srushti Sudhir Jagtap in 2023, when she was 16. Her performance focused mainly on kathak, one of India's major classical dance forms. Ben Dancer, 33, has been dancing professionally for 18 years. His attempt began on Tuesday 22 September and, if he completes the planned 168 hours, he is due to reach his target early on Tuesday morning. For much of the marathon, Ben Dancer has drawn on Nigeria's rich dance traditions as well as its fast-changing internet culture. Afrobeats has been a constant presence, alongside genres including fuji, jazz and zouk. At times, he has swapped his dance clothes for traditional Nigerian outfits, including the flowing agbada and dashiki. Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups, with a wide range of cultural traditions. Ben Dancer's team says the performance is intended to reflect that diversity, rather than simply test his physical endurance. His team says he underwent intensive fitness training before the attempt, changing his diet and focusing on carbohydrates and cardiovascular conditioning. During the marathon, he has been eating lightly and drinking fluids while taking the permitted five minutes of rest for every continuous hour of activity. Ben Dancer has chosen to dance for several hours at a time before taking his accumulated rest. A medical team has also been present at Freedom Park to provide assistance when needed. The scene around him has become something of a street party. Crowds of young people have gathered to cheer him on. Videos from the attempt have gone viral across social media platforms, drawing more people to the venue. Moronumubo Akodu, who has repeatedly visited to support Ben Dancer, said she was impressed by his determination but worried about the physical toll. "It is actually insane but I am so proud of him," she told the BBC. Emmanuel Ulelu, who visited the performance twice, said he noticed a striking change in the dancer's energy. "On day two, you could see the stress," he said. "Even after just three hours of dancing at the location myself, I wondered how he would keep going." But when he returned 16 hours into day five, he said Ben Dancer appeared more energetic than before. "It reminded me that we're capable of doing unbelievable things when how badly we want something matches and surpasses the difficulty of achieving it," he said. Nigeria has also developed a strong relationship with Guinness World Records, particularly in entertainment. In 2023, Nigerian chef Hilda Baci cooked continuously for 93 hours and 11 minutes in Lagos, which Guinness officially recognised as a new record. Her achievement sparked a surge of interest in record attempts in Nigeria, even though others have since surpassed her. Guinness says it received more than 1,500 new applications from the country within two months of her cook-a-thon, including events such as reading, singing, and crocheting. item.title: Iran court upholds lashes sentence for singer who performed without hijab
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn45ed1kqqgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Iran court upholds lashes sentence for singer who performed without hijab - Published An appeals court in Iran has confirmed a sentence of 74 lashes handed to a prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab, lawyers say. Parastoo Ahmadi sang while wearing a sleeveless dress during a concert livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024, external. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing. Iran's judiciary launched proceedings against the 29-year-old after the video went viral, gaining millions of views, saying the performance was "in violation of the country's legal and cultural regulations". In June, a criminal court in Qom reportedly found Ahmadi and eight members of her band and production team guilty of charges including "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material". In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years. On Friday, the defendants' appeal was "rejected" by a higher court without a hearing, according to their lawyers. "In our view, holding the concert was not a crime at all," one of the lawyers told the BBC. "The trial court imposed one of the harshest punishments for these charges, although fines and less severe penalties were also available." "The Court of Appeal, despite having the option of holding a hearing, did not hold a hearing and upheld the judgment. It appears that the main reason for issuing this judgment was to deter the recurrence of similar events." News of the initial sentence sparked widespread reaction among Iranians on social media. "May these dark days come to an end, and may women regain the freedom to choose how they live and dress, and may artistic expression once again flourish in our precious homeland," exiled singer Googoosh wrote on Instagram at the time. Musician Hossein Alizadeh meanwhile said he was "willing to take 70 lashes in Parastoo Ahmadi's place". Human rights activists also condemned the sentence, with Amnesty International warning that "flogging constitutes cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violates the absolute prohibition on torture and other ill treatment". In January 2024, Kurdish-Iranian activist Roya Heshmati was flogged 74 times after being convicted of "violating public morals" over a photo on social media that showed her without the hijab. She said a female officer forcibly placed a scarf on her head at a prosecutor's office in Tehran before a male officer whipped her shoulders, back, hips and legs, according to Kurdish rights group Hengaw, external. Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures. In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly". Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces. Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures. When discussing hijab enforcement earlier this month, conservative politician and Expediency Council member Gholamali Haddad‑Adel - who is also the father-in-law of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei - said that Iran's war with the US and Israel meant authorities "cannot engage on this front as much as we should for the time being". The war began at the end of February, only weeks after Iranian security forces had violently repressed another wave of mass protests sparked by the country's economic crisis, killing thousands of people. item.title: Stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8zxzlqwzw0eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan - Published An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan – and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months – but ordered his release due to time served. It has also placed him under a travel ban, preventing him from travelling outside Turkey. A final decision in the case will come from the court of appeals. Deniz Göktaş - who denied the charges - has already spent nearly 90 days in prison. Prosecutors had asked for up to 12 years. His case comes amid a wave of arrests in Turkey that human rights groups say is aimed at crushing dissent. His stand-up routine went viral on YouTube, attracting more than 15 million views. Prosecutors had singled out a line in which the comedian called the Turkish leader "a shy dictator", but Göktaş insisted there was "no criminal element" in his comments. "Dictator is not an insult," he said, "it is a political characterisation." But angering the president in Turkey is not funny. Göktaş was arrested and handcuffed at Istanbul airport in July when he returned from a holiday. During his court appearance on Monday, it was clear he did not lose his sense of humour during his 88 days in solitary confinement. "Three months have been taken away from my life," he said on the stand. "But I quit smoking, so I'll add another three months to my life." That drew laughter and loud applause in court. Outside, supporters like Firat Aksal – a fellow comedian – were very pleasantly surprised by the verdict. "We hardly know what to do with our happiness," he said. "We are thrilled. To be honest we weren't hopeful of getting a fair trial. " Göktaş was released at 21:45 local time (18:45 GMT) and greeted by well-wishers, including his parents who he was seen hugging, outside a prison facility. Aksal said Göktaş would now rest for a few days, and see his family, and then return to the stage. After his release, Göktaş told reporters: "I'm very happy to be reunited with my family, mother, father, and friends." But he added: "There are thousands of other people in prisons across Turkey. Some, like me, are being held in pre-trial detention, while others have been convicted because of their views. "So, of course, it's wonderful to be out. I've missed it very much. But there is not much difference between inside and outside. I hope the day comes when we can all regain our freedom together." Many others remain behind bars, including journalists, human rights campaigners, student protesters, LGBTQ activists, and the elected Mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem Imamoglu. Prisons are full in Turkey these days. Erdogan and his party in the past have denied arrests, such as that of Imamoglu, have been politically motivated, insisting that Turkey's judiciary is independent. item.title: Four bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan climbing group
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwjdvml9e897o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Four bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan climbing group - Published Rescuers have recovered four bodies from the site of an avalanche that struck a climbing group camping in the Nepalese part of the Himalayas. A dozen people are still thought to be missing after a sheet of snow fell on the base camp of Himlung Himal peak on Manang district on Sunday morning. The group of Nepalese nationals, including climbers and support staff, had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp and fix ropes. Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126m (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet. Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams initially unable to reach the site. Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told news agency AFP that at least eight members of his expedition team had been reported missing. A rescue team consisting of experienced mountaineers was rushed from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, via helicopter. On Sunday, the first two bodies were found, with another two bodies discovered on Monday, the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, which sent out a rescue team, said in a social media post. The group said the team ascended the mountain hoping to find survivors. "Unfortunately, after extensive search efforts under extremely difficult conditions, four bodies were recovered, while 12 cook staff remain missing at Himlung Base Camp." "The avalanche was exceptionally large, with approximately 14 feet of snow covering the Base Camp area. Searching every section manually was extremely difficult and dangerous due to the depth of snow, freezing temperatures, and unstable conditions." The group said it had temporarily paused operations due to the conditions, but will continue to monitor and "make every possible effort to recover the remaining bodies when it becomes safe to do so". The Nepalese team caught in the avalanche had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain. Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry. Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches. The latest death of Nepalese climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepalese mountaineer Nirmal Purja. It also comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August. More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements. Dangerous weather events have also affected other parts of Asia in the past week. Extreme weather in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has also killed more than 50 people, officials there said. Meanwhile, a flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok, Thailand because of heavy rainfall since Thursday, with people being urged to stay at home or move to higher floors. Earlier this week, a deadly typhoon that battered Tokyo, triggering landslides in neighbouring prefectures that killed four people. Typhoon Dujuan was the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", an area of warmer sea water that facilitates the formation of powerful storms. item.title: Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n9wrqpj4yqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back - Published Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by campaigners. The data centre was being developed by Goodman Group, Australia's biggest property company, and would have seen it construct a A$1.2bn (£630m; $841m), 90-megawatt facility known as Project Mars in the Lane Cove area. The company confirmed it was withdrawing its application in a letter to the local planning authority. It follows a concerted opposition against the data centre by local residents and campaigners. The dispute captures a wider disagreement in Australia over the role of data centres. With the mainstreaming of generative AI in recent years, there has been a huge swell in demand for data centres, and Australia - with its abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land - has become a global destination for their construction. However, while the country's government has been keen to attract investment from global AI companies, there has also been stiff opposition due to the huge demands the centres place on water and energy supplies, and the disruption they cause local communities. The proposal for Project Mars, which would have been constructed about 20 metres from the nearest house in the suburb of Lane Cove, received 374 submissions during a consultation - with just nine in support of it. According to local news website In the Cove, this is highest number of submissions ever received for a data centre application, external. In its letter to New South Wales Department of Planning, Goodman Group said since starting the planning process in March 2025, it had "undertaken extensive technical investigations, stakeholder engagement and community consultation". "During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said. It said it had "carefully considered these changes" along with the "views of the local community", and concluded it would not proceed with the development. The decision by Goodman Group follows an announcement by the New South Wales government last month that it would be introducing a fast-track programme for data centres. The programme would allow them to be assessed within 75 days, provided they meet requirements around certain standards and fund the additional supply of water and energy. In a message posted to the Facebook page of Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group, Anthony Roberts, a member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly representing Lane Cove, said it was "a huge win for the Lane Cove West community". "This is a common-sense win for our community," he said. "This victory sends a clear message to other data centre developers. To find suitable locations before putting proposals forward. "Data centres have an important role to play, but developments of this size and scale need to be appropriately located and planned with the surrounding community in mind." item.title: US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5wyzrm0n74ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University - Published New York state prosecutors say they will reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024. The woman filed a civil lawsuit on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped by multiple people at a fraternity house at the university. "Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said Monday. Cornell University said that while it supported the case being brought before a grand jury, "any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false". The woman, referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges in her lawsuit that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter allegedly assaulted her in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine. Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and was incapable of providing consent. She said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024. The lawsuit also contains an image purported to be from a Snapchat fraternity group chat, in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Jane Doe. Van Houten said on Monday that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from her statement to authorities did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges. He said he reached out to Jane Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury. In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges. In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Jane Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack. He noted the statement differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit. "Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday. "On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual." Van Houten added that Jane Doe's lawyers had never been in touch with him to say her original statement was inaccurate or to ask him to reconsider his decision not to bring charges. He later acknowledged "the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them". The BBC has contacted Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. In a statement on Monday obtained by CBS, the BBC's US partner, he said: "In the days following the assault, [Jane Doe] was traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode." Giuffra said Jane Doe never spoke to anyone other than the officer who took her initial complaint, adding: "I would have expected at the very least that she would have been interviewed several times and evidence collected by law enforcement and a case developed. This is the normal sequence for serious crime investigations." "The defensive posture I have gleaned from the DA's statements leads me to believe that they recognise that there were failures and they are trying to excuse them," he said. Jane Doe also alleged in her civil lawsuit that Cornell did not protect her nor adequately punish the men involved, alleging they were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays". Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the incident and the university's handling, the suit states, adding that news of the incident quickly circulated through the school. In November 2024, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house", saying its campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students." Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law - which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities. On Monday, the university disputed Jane Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators. The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell". "None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," Cornell said. Jeremy Saland, an attorney for one of the men named in the lawsuit, denied the allegations. Saland acknowledged his client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat", but "did nothing else." Saland denied his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine". The case has received national attention following Doe's lawsuit and the announcement the case would be reopened. Several celebrities, including actress Florence Pugh, have spoken out about it. If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. item.title: Remains of dozens of suspected kidnap victims found in Nigerian forests
item.description:

Remains of dozens of suspected kidnap victims found in Nigerian forests - Published The skulls and bones of at least 28 people have been recovered from suspected criminal camps in Nigerian forests. Police in the south-eastern state of Abia are investigating the identities of the remains found in the Umuaku and Nneato forests on Saturday after a security operation was carried out in the Umunneochi area. Police spokeswoman Maureen Chinaka said the suspects fled when police arrived. The discovery is likely to revive concerns about kidnapping gangs operating in remote forests across parts of south-eastern Nigeria, where criminal groups have frequently targeted motorists, travellers and residents for ransom. According to Abia State Police Command, the raids were launched following intelligence reports about suspected criminal activity in the forests. Officers suspect the remains belong to kidnapping victims, although forensic and other investigations are ongoing to establish their identities and the circumstances surrounding their deaths. "Upon arrival of the Command's tactical operatives at the camps, the suspects fled. The criminal camps were subsequently dismantled. A total of twenty-eight human skulls and bones, suspected to be kidnap victims, were recovered," Chinaka said in a statement. Police said surveillance had been intensified in the area as officers sought to track down those who fled. Abia state police commissioner Wilfred Afolabi said the operation was part of an ongoing campaign to dismantle criminal hideouts in the state. Police have appealed to residents to report suspicious activity and security concerns as efforts continue to identify the victims and determine whether the remains are connected to unresolved kidnapping cases in the region. Authorities have previously discovered decomposing bodies believed to be linked to kidnapping activities during security raids in Umunneochi. Separately over the weekend, more than 80 people, mostly women, were seized in separate mass kidnappings in two states in the country's north. In an attack on Sunday, nearly 50 farmers were abducted by gunmen in Niger State. On Sunday, about 40 other women were kidnapped in the neighbouring state of Zamfara, according to two security reports seen by AFP and a local source. Abductions for ransom have become a key source of income for criminals, including bandits and militant Islamists, in northern Nigeria. - Published29 December 2025

Mexico's Pacific coast braces for Hurricane Polo - Published People living on the northern Pacific coast of Mexico are bracing for the arrival of Hurricane Polo, which is forecast to make landfall later on Monday or early on Tuesday. The category three storm, with maximum sustained winds near 115 mph (185 km/h), is expected to move over the state of Baja California Sur, a region popular with tourists and home to the resort destination of Los Cabos. Meteorologists at the US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) have warned of heavy rainfall which could lead to life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain. Residents on Sunday stocked up on essentials such as drinking water and food as the storm approached. The NHC warned of the storm surge Hurricane Polo could unleash, which it said could be accompanied by large and destructive waves. In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, the authorities restricted access to the beaches. Some restaurants also closed in the town, which acts as a base for sport fishers and whale watchers. The regional government of Baja California Sur has ordered schools to remain closed on Monday as a preventive measure. Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío said temporary shelters had been opened should residents need to be evacuated. item.title: Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxp84g2ly1mjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump-Xi summit: What wasn't said might matter the most - Published On Monday, China released more information of what was agreed at the talks between Xi Jinping and Donald Tump last week, shedding light on a handful of concrete outcomes. But there were no joint statements and few major breakthroughs. Instead, both governments issued separate accounts of the meeting - perhaps a sign that despite the White House tours and promise of warmer ties, Washington and Beijing remain wary of each other. Here are four things we now know - and still don't - about what transpired at the talks. A new AI dialogue and communication channel Beijing says it has agreed with Washington to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for the end of November. As both countries race to develop advanced artificial intelligence, the move suggests they see a need for some guardrails around a technology that is increasingly being used in everything from business to military planning. They have also agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents, aimed at preventing misunderstandings or unexpected developments from turning into a broader confrontation. The meeting was being closely watched for any developments or agreements in relation to AI - especially in the wake of calls by US companies like Anthropic to slow down developments, and revelations that Open AI had gained unauthorised access to government websites in countries like Australia and had "meddled" with multiple US government agency sites. - Huge data centres rise at 'China speed' to power its AI ambitions - Published6 days ago - Trump and Xi come face-to-face as US and China battle to win the AI race - Published5 days ago - Trump wants AI to be rebranded as super intelligence. Will it work? - Published5 days ago Trade truce - what was included and what was left out Chinese state media confirmed for the first time on Monday that the trade truce has been extended until 10 January. The short extension ensures both leaders will meet again at major international gatherings later this year. Trump will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November while Xi is due to travel to Miami for the G20 summit in December. It is rare for the leaders of the world's two largest economies to meet so frequently. But Beijing had hoped for a much longer extension to the truce, making the two month reprieve a modest gain rather than a major breakthrough. China did secure lower tariffs on $30bn (£23bn) of goods entering the US with reciprocal reductions expected from Beijing. Chinese products heading to American stores ranging from toys to small household appliances to Christmas decorations will benefit from the lower tariffs. The Trump administration also said Beijing would buy at least 10 million metric tons of coal annually in 2027 and 2028. What is striking is what was left out. There was no mention of increasing exports of China's rare earth minerals to the US nor was there any indication that restrictions on advanced US semiconductors would be eased. The US left out Taiwan - but China didn't The White House factsheet made no mention of Taiwan, but the issue was clearly a priority for Xi Jinping. According to Beijing's accounts of the talks, Xi urged Donald Trump to formally oppose Taiwan independence and handle the issue with caution. After their previous meeting in May, Trump revealed that Xi directly asked him if the US would defend Taiwan in the event of a Chinese attack. He told reporters, "There's only one person that knows that, and it is me," and he raised the question whether it made sense for US forces to "travel 9,500 miles to fight a war" over the issue. This time, Trump disclosed far less. "We didn't talk about it too much," he told reporters over the weekend. "Right now, it's fine. It's just moving along," Trump said. "He understands very much how I feel." That silence may be significant. Trump has previously described a proposed $14bn US arms package for Taiwan as "a very good negotiating chip" in his dealings with Beijing. The arms package has been on hold for months. Adding to the confusion, US Ambassador to China David Perdue told Fox News that Trump had offered to sell weapons to Xi during the summit. The State Department later clarified that US law prohibits arms sales to China and there are no plans to do so. Beijing sees the self-governing island as part of China. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. China may be opening the investment doors China says it will allow more foreign financial firms, including American-backed banks, investment companies and insurers, to apply to do business and open offices in China. But any approvals will still be subject to Chinese laws and regulations. The last line is key. China is opening the door, but still controls who gets through it. Foreign financial firms have long complained that regulatory barriers, licensing requirements and concerns over exit bans make it difficult to expand in China, even when market access is technically allowed. Beijing also said it was discussing ways to increase the number of flights between both countries, but neither side has explained how this would happen. And despite giving visa free entry to visitors from more than 75 countries across the world, China has not extended that offer to Americans. Meanwhile the US State Department continues to classify travel to China as a Level 2 advisory urging travellers to "exercise increased caution" because of the risk of arbitrary law enforcement, exit bans and detention. So even though both sides are talking about encouraging business and travel some of the biggest obstacles remain firmly in place. So what do we know? This summit produced more dialogue - but very little decision change for now. The most contentious issues from advanced technology to Taiwan remain unresolved. But for both leaders, this is a familiar outcome - a promise of more channels of communication, modest economic concessions and modest proposals to steady relations. And while both remain committed to a steady relationship - continued US-China dialogue appears far easier than asking either superpower to compromise. - Published25 August 2025

item.title: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckpq0g7z5pjjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections - Published Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption. Aleksandar Vučić said his administration had preserved peace and stability during his nine-year tenure as he addressed supporters outside the presidential building in the capital, Belgrade. He had already announced his intention to resign in June and is currently standing to be his party's candidate for prime minister in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Vučić cannot run for a third presidential term under Serbia's constitution. The populist leader's administration has been dogged by anger over alleged corner-cutting. It was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station's roof, killing 16 people, that first galvanised anger towards the government in 2024. Protests involving a wide range of citizens - from students and teachers to workers and farmers - followed. Demonstrators believed that the disaster reflected more than a decade of governing by the Progressive Party of Vucic, who closely associated himself with the station's renovation, which was supposed to be a symbol of Serbia's progress. A series of resignations of those under the embattled president failed to placate the protesters, who continued to demonstrate throughout this summer, turning to unrest following accusations of police brutality. Vučić's presidency was due to expire next year. Under Serbia's constitution, presidential elections must be held no more than three months after his resignation. This means Serbians will go to the polls twice before the end of the year. Vučić said the presidential election will take place more than a month after the snap parliamentary election in late October, itself called in response to the protests, which had added calls for a vote to their list of demands. He had earlier announced that he planned to run in that election as Progressive Party's leader, leaving the possibility he could retain a position at the top of Serbian politics. Parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić, also a Progressive Party member, will assume the role of interim president until a new one is elected. Vučić used his constitutional powers to pardon 49 people, including 23 students and party loyalists suspected of offences related to what he called the "terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half", according to Serbian public broadcaster RTS. The upcoming parliamentary elections will pit Vučić's Progressive Party against a student-led, anti-corruption movement called Students Win and a coalition of pro-Western opposition parties known as European Serbia. Vucic has been a fixture of Serbian politics for more than a decade, becoming prime minister in 2014, before being elected to his first term as president in 2017. He has publicly said he wants Serbia to join the EU while courting close ties with Russia and opening Serbia up to Chinese investment. One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey - Published Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events. The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine. In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree. The man has been identified as 56-year-old Leighton Brown, an employee of the New York City Housing Authority. According to local news, he was walking through east Brooklyn neighbourhood working an extra shift when the deadly incident occurred. "We mourn deeply for the loss of Leighton Brown, a NYCHA employee who faithfully served Brooklyn residents and who was known for his warm personality," the Office of the NYC Public Advocate wrote on social media. The nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 160,000 households, nearly all in the north-eastern US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage. More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware. A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday. NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines. "Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater." In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead. Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather. Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said. item.description:

========================================
Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow - Published Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President Donald Trump in New York. Among those released in the early hours of Saturday morning was Wilder Vasquez, who was handed a five-year sentence in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill former President Nicolás Maduro. Opposition figures have renewed calls for free elections after interim President Delcy Rodriguez held talks with Trump, who captured Maduro earlier this year, at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday. Her administration previously released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure. However, these releases slowed to a trickle in April after Rodriguez said the scheme was "coming to an end". Venezuela's government has not made any statement concerning the latest releases, nor has it indicated whether they were the result of her conversation with the US president. Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of rights group Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released on Saturday morning from several of Venezuela's detention centres. Foro Penal confirmed the release of Miguel Castillo Cedeño, who it said had been arbitrarily detained since June 2019. Also released was Frank Cabañas, who rights groups say had been held in prison for nine years after being linked to the death of a police officer. Foro Penal said he was the only suspect who remained detained, despite family members reporting that he was suffering health problems last year. Opposition and human rights groups have said Maduro's government used the detention of political prisoners to stamp out dissent and silence critics for years. Rodriguez has sought to frame her interim government as more permissive of political dissent while currying favour with the US. The prisoner release scheme was a key concession by her administration to the US. However, her decision to end the scheme attracted criticism from opposition and rights groups. Foro Penal said it was stopped with less than half of the nation's political prisoners released. Rodriguez's government continues to deny dissidents are jailed. It has cast the release of prisoners as a gesture of goodwill and reconciliation. Venezuelan Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a minister closely associated with Maduro's authoritarian rule, called the interim president's meeting with Trump "a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace". But opposition voices expressed their disapproval over the meeting, viewing it as a snub of their calls – that the US has previously endorsed – for swift elections. Pedro Mario Burelli, a former Venezuelan state oil company executive and opposition commentator, called the two world leaders "the shameless puppet and her unscrupulous and undignified puppet-master", adding: "Little has changed in Venezuela under Washington's clumsy and selective oversight." Venezuela's last elections, held in 2024, in which Maduro was declared the winner, were widely disputed as rigged. Opposition tallies suggested their candidate, who stood after Machado was barred from running, had won by 70% of the vote. Despite this, the Trump administration backed Rodriguez, Maduro's former vice-president, as his successor rather than opposition leader María Corina Machado after Maduro was seized and put on trial on drug charges in January. Analysts at the time cast this decision as the US choosing short-term stability in Venezuela until elections could be held. Rodriguez used her UN General Assembly speech on Thursday to reiterate that there "will be elections in Venezuela", without specifying when. Pope says 'scourge' of abuse must be rooted out as he visits Lourdes - Published Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vigilance". The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France. A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years. The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes before later meeting survivors of abuse. The Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context. "It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance." The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters. Leo then met with seven survivors of abuse by the French clergy. The Pope "thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others", the Vatican said in a statement. "It was extraordinary," said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos at a news conference following the encounter with the pontiff. He said Leo listened and was informed of their cases. "I never thought I would have a Pope before me," he added. The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak. Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile. On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron. During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed". The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church". "How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said. The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000. But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025. Sexual abuse inside the Catholic Church has been widespread and dates back to the 1950s. The issue was first given significant media attention in the 1980s in the US and Canada before similar stories emerged across the world, including widespread historic abuse in Ireland and the UK. Reporting by the Boston Globe newspaper in the early 2000s, dramatised in the 2015 film Spotlight, exposed widespread abuse and how paedophile priests were moved around by Church leaders instead of being held accountable. It prompted people to come forward across the US and around the world. A Church-commissioned report in 2004 said more than 4,000 US Roman Catholic priests had faced sexual abuse allegations in the last 50 years, in cases involving more than 10,000 children - mostly boys. Leo's predecessor Pope Francis tried to address the issue by holding an unprecedented summit on paedophilia in the Church, and by changing its laws to explicitly criminalise sexual abuse, but problems remain. Later on Sunday, the Pope met staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, and took part in a torchlight procession. It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic Church in May 2025. Popes have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots. - Published3 days ago - Published3 days ago

item.title: Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm750plvwy9vo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality - Published Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality. More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed. The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment. Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties. Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia. "People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said. Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility". While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference". He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace". Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe. This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv. Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees. Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s. Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal - Published Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping within seven days because "they're losing so badly". In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response. He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past. Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran that was signed in June. Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week. The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February. "I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers. Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently". He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them." Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York for the UN general assembly, told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful. He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government". Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?" He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face. Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks. Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis. Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway. Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker. Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage". "President Trump's right to reject it," he said. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic sanctions imposed by the US were taking a toll on Iran. Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran. The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran "Operation Economic Outcast", with the White House attempting to use economic pressure to force Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners. These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran. Related topics - Published5 days ago

item.title: Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim too
item.description:
